title: Self-Paced Module: Java Threads and Concurrency Tools

lessons.title: One Terminal, Many Dispatchers: Threads with Thread, start(), and join()

objectives.cognitive: Explain what a thread is, how it differs from a process, and why a program must call start() and not run().
objectives.affective: Value other people's time by letting independent work happen together instead of making everyone wait in one line.
objectives.psychomotor: Write DispatchThread, start three threads, join them, and print the results in a fixed order; show the difference between start() and run().

blocks.markdown:
**Where we left off:** your folder should already have `Vehicle.java`, `Jeepney.java`, `Tricycle.java`, `Bus.java`, `OverloadException.java`, `InvalidDistanceException.java`, and `VehicleNotFoundException.java`. Save a copy of `Main.java` as `Main_week15.txt`. (There was no class on Monday, November 2, All Souls' Day.)

**The problem this week fixes:** every program so far does **one thing at a time**. If it waits for a slow job, everything else waits too. Java can do many things at once with **threads**.

**No internet needed.** Keep every class in its own file, all in one folder. Compile with `javac *.java`, run with `java Main`. Output order depends on short pauses (0.1 to 0.4 seconds); on a very slow computer a line or two could appear in a different order.

A **process** is a program that is running, with its own memory. A **thread** is one line of work **inside** a process. Every Java program starts with one thread, called `main`. Your program can start more threads; they run **at the same time** and **share** the process's memory. Threads of the same process can see the same objects; two different processes cannot.

The **terminal** is the process: one building, one logbook, one set of vehicles. The **dispatchers** are the threads. With one dispatcher (`main`), every job waits for the one before it. With three, one can load passengers, one can collect fares, one can call the next jeepney, all in the same terminal. The risk: two dispatchers writing in the same line of the logbook at once. So this week, **each thread uses only its own data**.

lessons.title: Job Orders and Roll Calls: Runnable and CountDownLatch

objectives.cognitive: Describe what a Runnable is and how a CountDownLatch makes one thread wait for several others.
objectives.affective: Show responsibility by making sure every job reports back, even when something goes wrong.
objectives.psychomotor: Write a Runnable job and give it to a Thread; write ReadyReport and use a CountDownLatch so main waits for four reports.

blocks.markdown: An **interface**: a promise that a class has certain methods. This one has just one, `void run()`. A class that **implements Runnable** describes **a job**. To get it done, hand the job to a `Thread`: `new Thread(job, "name")`. This is the usual way, because the job class can still extend another class, but a class can extend only one parent, and `Thread` would use it up.

`extends Thread` is like hiring a person **who comes with one job fixed to them**. `Runnable` is writing the job on a **work order** ("load these groups of passengers") and giving it to any available worker. The worker is the `Thread`, the order is the `Runnable`.

rows: a job class with run(), then new Thread(job)
Can the class extend another class?

blocks.instruction: Make `BoardingTask.java`, then replace `Main.java`. It uses Week 13's `board()` and `OverloadException`: each job catches its **own** exception.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Jeep loader: all boarded
Trike loader: stopped: TRC 456 is full! Capacity 4, but 5 tried to ride.
NXA 123 | Driver: Mang Ramon | Passengers: 19/20
TRC 456 | Driver: Kuya Ben | Passengers: 4/4

activity.instruction: Change the Tricycle groups from {2, 2, 1} to {1, 1, 1}. It should finish normally with three passengers. Keep the Jeepney groups unchanged.

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** the trike's job stopped when 5 people tried to ride a 4-seat tricycle (Week 13's `OverloadException`), but the jeepney's job was not affected. A job that catches its own problems cannot hurt the others.

Starts with a number, such as 4. Each worker calls `countDown()` when it is done, which lowers the number by 1. A thread that calls `await()` **waits until the number is 0**, then goes on. A latch is **one-shot**: once at 0, it cannot be reset.

The dispatcher says, "We leave when **4** vehicles report ready." Each driver radios in when ready. The dispatcher keeps a tally: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. At 0 she blows the whistle. It does not matter **who** reports first, only that all 4 have.

Dispatcher waits. Reports still needed: 4
TRC 456 reports: ready
NYB 321 reports: ready
BUS 789 reports: ready
NXA 123 reports: ready
Reports still needed: 0

blocks.checkYourself: Change `new CountDownLatch(4)` to `(5)` and run. Only 4 jobs call `countDown()`, so the count stops at 1 and the program **never ends**. Press Ctrl+C to stop it, then change it back.

activity.instruction: Use a CountDownLatch of three and remove the BUS 789 worker. Remove worker-thread ready/interruption prints from ReadyReport. After await(), print only the remaining count and final dispatch message. Remove the initial dispatcher/count print; scheduling must not decide the output.
activity.expectedOutput:

blocks.markdown: **Read it carefully:** the reports come in order of **speed** (TRC 100 ms first, NXA 400 ms last), not the order the threads were started. `countDown()` sits in `finally` (Week 13) so the count goes down even if something goes wrong in the job. Without it, `await()` could wait forever.

questions.prompt: What is a `Runnable`? How do you get a Runnable job done (Step 4)? Give one reason it is often better than `extends Thread`.
In Step 4, the tricycle's job stopped with an `OverloadException`, but the jeepney's job finished normally. Why did one stopped job not stop the other?
In Step 5, `latch.countDown()` is inside `finally`. Which Week 13 idea is this? What could happen to `await()` if it were not there and a job failed?

lessons.title: Convoys and Loading Bays: CyclicBarrier and Semaphore

objectives.cognitive: Differentiate CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, and Semaphore, and say which one fits a given situation.
objectives.affective: Practice fairness by letting limited resources, such as loading bays, be shared in turn.
objectives.psychomotor: Write ConvoyLeg with a CyclicBarrier used at two stops, and LoadingBay with a Semaphore of two permits.

blocks.markdown: A `CyclicBarrier(3)` makes a group of **3** threads wait at a meeting point. Each calls `await()`. When the **3rd** arrives, all three are released together, and the barrier is **ready to use again**. `await()` gives back a number: **0 for the last thread to arrive**. Difference from a latch: here the **workers wait for each other**, and the barrier can be reused.
Three jeepneys travel as a **convoy**. At every stop they wait for each other, and leave only when all three have arrived. At the next stop they wait for each other again. One barrier, reused.

blocks.instruction: Make `ConvoyLeg.java`, then replace `Main.java`. It also needs `BrokenBarrierException`, a checked exception that `await()` can throw.
blocks.expectedOutput:
NYB 321 arrived at Monumento
BUS 789 arrived at Monumento
NXA 123 arrived at Monumento
-- All here at Monumento. The convoy moves on together!

NXA 123 arrived at Recto

blocks.checkYourself: Change `CyclicBarrier(3)` to `(4)`. Only 3 vehicles exist, so all three wait at Monumento **forever** (Ctrl+C to stop). Change it back.

Number its two releases as "Convoy release 1" and "Convoy release 2"; keep the final Convoy finished message.

Convoy finished.

blocks.markdown: A `Semaphore(2)` holds **2 permits**. `acquire()` takes one permit, or **waits** if none is left. `release()` gives one back. So at most 2 threads are in the protected part at once. `availablePermits()` tells how many are free. Put `release()` in `finally` so a permit is never lost.
The terminal has **2 loading bays**. A vehicle that arrives takes a bay if one is free; otherwise it waits in line. When a vehicle leaves, it frees its bay for the next one. The permits are the bays.

rows: a meeting point for a group

lessons.title: Many Helpers at Once: Threads Performance Task and Presentation

objectives.cognitive: Justify the choice of threads and of waiting tools in their own program.
objectives.affective: Show respect for classmates' work by testing each other's programs fairly and giving helpful feedback during presentations.
objectives.psychomotor: Build, test four ways, and present a program with three or more helper threads, a latch, and a second tool, without crashing or hanging.

blocks.markdown: Today you finish and present the **Performance Task**: give your own program helpers that work at the same time. Run it four ways before you present, then answer the Friday exit slip.

questions.prompt: Name two of your helpers (threads). Write the line of your code that starts one of them, and the line that waits for it or for all of them.
You used a `CountDownLatch` and a second tool (`Semaphore` or `CyclicBarrier`). Defend each choice. What would go wrong if you swapped them?
The school canteen has 3 cashiers who serve students at the same time, and the canteen opens only when all 3 are ready. Which of this week's tools would you use for each need, and why?
Compare your programs before this week, where one thing happened at a time, with now. What can your program do now that it could not before? What part was hardest?

performanceTask.title: Performance Task: Make Your Program Do Many Things at Once
performanceTask.markdown:
Open your own program from your Four Pillars Performance Task (your sari-sari store, pets, gadgets, school personnel, or shapes theme). Give it **helpers that work at the same time**, and make them wait for each other the right way. Start on Thursday after the Thursday exit slip; finish and present on Friday.

**Reuse this week's code.** Your helper class works like `BoardingTask` (Step 4) or `DispatchThread` (Step 1); the latch like Step 5; the barrier like Step 6; the semaphore like Step 7. The example shows only the latch: **you must add a second tool.**

**Example (sari-sari store, two cashiers):**

- Ana rang up Bread P12
- Ben rang up Soap P18
- Ana rang up Rice P55
- Ben rang up Coffee P9
- Ana's total: P67 / Ben's total: P27 / Store total: P94

**Testing tip:** run your program at least four ways: (1) normally; (2) three times in a row: the totals must be identical; (3) change one sleep time: the order of messages changes, but the totals do not; (4) give one helper bad data: it must be caught and the others must still finish. No run may end in `Exception in thread "main"`, and none may hang.

**Plan before you type** (show your teacher): for each helper, write its name, whether it is a Thread or a Runnable, its job, its own data, and which tool joins it in, and why.
steps: In Projects, click **Personal performance-task project**. Your own program opens.
On paper, for each helper write its name, whether it is a Thread or a Runnable, its job, its own data, and which tool waits for it, and why. Show your teacher.
Add a helper class file. Copy **Step 4 · BoardingTask.java** (Runnable) or **Step 1 · DispatchThread.java** (Thread), paste it, and change it for your theme. Give each helper a name that is printed.
In `main`, make at least 3 helpers and begin each with `start()`, never `run()`, like **Step 2 · Main.java**. Each helper changes only its own data.
Use `Thread.sleep()` to show that work takes time, and handle every `InterruptedException`.
Add a `CountDownLatch`: `countDown()` in `finally` inside each helper, and `await()` in `main`, like **Step 5 · ReadyReport.java**. **Sample code · Cashier.java** shows the store example.
Add a second tool that fits your story: a `Semaphore`, like **Step 7 · LoadingBay.java**, or a `CyclicBarrier`, like **Step 6 · ConvoyLeg.java**.
Print the results after everyone has finished, in a fixed order, like **Step 3 · Main.java**.
Give one helper bad data and catch it inside its `run()`. The other helpers must still finish.
Test four ways: normally; three times in a row (same totals); with one sleep time changed (order changes, totals do not); with bad data in one helper. No run may crash or hang.
Add a comment on each part, for example `// LATCH: store opens when both cashiers finish`.
Tick each item in the **Performance task checklist**, then click **Submit this version**.
checklist: At least 3 helper objects from your theme, each doing its own job on its own thread
Helpers built with extends Thread or implements Runnable; each has a name that is printed
Each thread changes only its own data, no shared variable
A CountDownLatch, with countDown() in finally, and await() in main
A second tool: Semaphore or CyclicBarrier, with a story that fits your theme
Thread.sleep() shows work takes time; every InterruptedException is handled
Results are printed after everyone has finished, in a fixed order
Bad data in one helper is caught inside its run(); the others still finish
A comment on each part, e.g. // LATCH: store opens when both cashiers finish
presentationOutline: Introduce your theme and your helpers. (30 sec)
Run it and show the output. (1 min)
Prove it live: run it again; change a sleep; break it on purpose. (2 min)
Point to the code for a thread, the latch, and the second tool. (1 min)
questionsToPrepare: What does your latch count? What if the number is too big?
Why print the totals after the threads finish?
What could go wrong if two threads changed one variable?

rubric.criterion: Threads: 3+ helpers started with start(); named; finish before results are shown
Design: Thread or Runnable used correctly; each thread keeps its own data
Tools: latch used correctly; a second tool that fits the story
Results: same correct totals on every run, in a fixed order
Errors: InterruptedException and bad data handled; no crash, no hang
